newsitem.title: USA: Hepatitis inoculations continue in Michigan.
newsitem.headline: Hepatitis inoculations continue in Michigan.

text.p: Michigan officials said Thursday the frozen strawberries that caused an outbreak of hepatitis A virus among school children may have also been distributed to restaurants and retail outlets.
Previously, federal officials have said they believed the strawberries packaged by Andrew & Williamson Sales Co. of San Diego had only been sent to the government's school lunch programme.

"State officials have just learned that Caramagno Foods Co. of Detroit did receive frozen strawberries direct from Andrew & Williamson outside of the school lunch programme," the Michigan Department of Agriculture said in a statement.
Geralyn Lasher, a spokeswoman for the department, said the exact number of frozen strawberries distributed by Caramagno is not known, although it is believed to be small.

The berries were distributed by the company to retaurants, wholesalers and retail locations in 6-1/2 pound plastic containers labeled with the Andrew & Williamson seal from May 17, 1996, until December 31, 1996.
"We believe at this point, because of the distribution date, that most of these strawberries were consumed some time ago," said Dan Wyant, director of the department.

Also on Thursday, state officials increased to 175 from 153 the number of hepatitis A cases that have been confirmed. Of the six states that received possibly contaminated berries, Michigan is the only one to have a confirmed outbreak.
Since the beginning of March, about 160 cases have been identified in Calhoun County, and about 15 were identified in Saginaw County.
The strawberries were distributed as frozen desserts to schools in 28 counties in Michigan. About 1,300 30-pound (13 kilogram) containers are believed to have been sent.

Michigan officials cautioned the full extent of the problem may not be known for a few more weeks since the berries were still being consumed late last week. Hepatitis A takes between two and six weeks to develop. The illness is rarely fatal but can cause fever, nausea, abdominal pain and jaundice.
Among those who were served the desserts were about 1,400 people who attended a Special Olympics event in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on March 22.

Throughout Michigan school children and adults continued to line up Thursday for inoculations with an immune globulin. Although not a vaccine, the globulin contains antibodies to help prevent the illness.
However, it is only effective for 14 days from the time the illness was contracted, meaning people who ate the berries weeks ago would not be helped.
Dennis Bandy, Special Olympics coordinator for Southgate, Michigan, said that about 30 people on his teams ate the berries at the Special Olympics event.
"The kids are taking it pretty good. Nobody panicked," Bandy said of the inoculation programme "As long as the adults don't panic, the kids aren't going to panic."
